title: Your first Blyx program
summary: Start in the browser, make a prediction, then edit and run your first line of Blyx.

sections.heading: Start with a running file
sections.text: A program is a set of instructions written as text. The editor below contains a complete file. Select Run program and read the Output pane. If Run on edit is selected, changes run automatically. You can reset the example at any time.

sections.heading: Read the greeting
sections.text: The two lines beginning with // are notes for the reader. Execution begins at fn main(). The braces enclose the work that main performs. Inside them, println! writes the text between the double quotes and finishes the line. The semicolon ends that instruction.

sections.heading: Change one thing
sections.text: Replace World inside the quoted greeting with your name. Leave the quotes, parentheses, exclamation mark and semicolon where they are. Run again and compare the two greetings. Changing the text changes what your reader sees.

sections.heading: Let the computer calculate
sections.text: Add println!(6 * 7); on a new line inside the braces. Blyx evaluates the multiplication before printing 42. Put double quotes around 6 * 7 and you will see the characters instead. The difference between a value and text describing a value will recur throughout the course.

exercise.prompt: Make the program print Hello, Blyx! on its first line and 42 on its second.
exercise.hint: Keep both print calls inside main. Use quotes for the greeting and leave the multiplication unquoted.
exercise.answer: Each println! adds one line. The arithmetic expression evaluates before the second call.

title: Numbers and expressions
summary: Use a packing problem to learn whole numbers, decimals, operator order and integer division.

sections.heading: Turn a question into an expression
sections.text: How many rows of five can you fill with 23 items? Give the two counts names with let. Since both values are integers, items / row yields the number of whole rows. The remainder operator, %, gives the three items still on the table.

sections.heading: Choose whole or fractional units
sections.text: The literal 23 has type i64, a signed 64-bit integer. The literal 23.0 has type f64, a 64-bit floating-point number. The expression 23.0 / 5.0 yields 4.6. Use integer counts for indivisible objects and decimal operands on both sides when a fraction matters.

sections.heading: Group an expression
sections.text: Multiplication and division bind more tightly than addition and subtraction. Read 2 + 3 * 4 as 2 + (3 * 4), which gives 14. In the editor, parentheses make (2 + 3) happen first, giving 20.

sections.heading: Choose useful test cases
sections.text: A full row, one fewer than a full row, and zero items each tell you something different about the result. With a nonzero row size, full_rows * row + leftover reconstructs the input. Integer division by zero and integer overflow produce execution errors.

exercise.prompt: Pack 24 items in rows of five. Predict both integer results before running.
exercise.hint: The division and remainder use items. The separate decimal example uses literal values.
exercise.answer: Four complete rows hold 20 items. Four items remain. The decimal expression and the grouped expression still use their original literals.

title: Text, comments and output
summary: Build a receipt one value at a time and learn how strings differ from variable names.

sections.heading: Name the pieces
sections.text: A string literal encloses text in double quotes. Inside "Total: " the final space separates the label from the price. Outside quotes, label refers to the value introduced by let. Writing "label" would print those five letters.

sections.heading: Assemble a line
sections.text: print!(label) writes the label and leaves the cursor on that line. println!(cost) writes the integer and ends the line. The last call starts a new line with Paid. To display several values together, use consecutive calls. These macros take zero or one expression.

sections.heading: Write a useful comment
sections.text: A // comment continues to the end of its line. A comment such as // price is in whole credits records the unit that the number alone cannot express. Put the calculation in a binding if you want to print it twice.

sections.heading: Read output precisely
sections.text: An extra space, a missing line break or putting the numeric expression inside quotes can change a report. First compare the lines and then compare characters within each line. This is the same approach you can use when testing a longer program.

exercise.prompt: Change the quantity from three to five and replace the final receipt line with Thanks.
exercise.hint: Edit the expression that defines cost, then edit the last quoted string.
exercise.answer: Five units at seven credits cost 35. print! keeps the label and total on the same line.

title: Bindings, mutation and scope
summary: Trace a name through nested blocks and choose when a value should change.

sections.heading: Bind a name
sections.text: let level = 3; evaluates the right-hand expression and gives its result a name. An immutable binding is a useful default for a quantity that should keep the same value. Declare let mut when later statements need to update that particular binding.

sections.heading: Follow a name into a block
sections.text: At the opening brace the program enters a new scope. The inner let level = 8; creates a second binding. A read of level starts in the current scope, so the first print sees 8. Leaving the block removes the inner binding and the outer 3 is visible again.

sections.heading: Change an existing binding
sections.text: An assignment starts with the name, as in level = 8;. The interpreter finds the nearest binding with that name. Assignment requires a mutable binding and a compatible value kind. If there is an inner declaration, updating it only changes the inner value.

sections.heading: Accumulate a result
sections.text: For a mutable integer counter, count += 1 adds one to the current value. The same updates work for subtraction, multiplication, division and remainder through -=, *=, /= and %=. Start a sum at zero and a product at one so the initial value preserves the first term.

exercise.prompt: Make both print calls show 8 by updating the outer level inside the block.
exercise.hint: Use mut for the outer declaration and remove let from the inner statement.
exercise.answer: There is now one mutable binding. The assignment reaches it and the new value is still visible after the block.

title: Booleans and decisions
summary: Classify temperatures, then test exactly what happens at the boundaries.

sections.heading: Ask a yes-or-no question
sections.text: A comparison such as t < 0.0 produces true or false. An if condition requires a boolean. The band function first checks for a value below zero. Its early return immediately sends the string frozen back to the caller.

sections.heading: Partition the remaining inputs
sections.text: After the first check, every remaining input in this example is zero or warmer. The final if expression chooses mild below 30 and hot otherwise. Because this expression supplies the function’s result, there is no semicolon after its closing brace.

sections.heading: Read the comparison signs
sections.text: Use == to compare for equality and != to test inequality. Use < or > for strict limits and <= or >= to include the limit itself. To combine rules, && requires both sides, || requires at least one, and ! reverses a boolean. Short-circuit evaluation skips the right side once the answer is known.

sections.heading: Test the boundary
sections.text: Two implementations can agree on -2 and 10 and still disagree at zero. A boundary test deliberately uses the threshold itself. Here 0.0 skips the frozen branch and 30.0 skips the mild branch.

exercise.prompt: Change the rule so exactly 30 is mild. Keep the boundary at zero as it is.
exercise.hint: Look for the comparison in the final if expression.
exercise.answer: Including equality sends 30.0 through the mild branch. The negative and zero cases take their original branches.

title: Functions, parameters and results
summary: Give a calculation a name, call it more than once, and use its return value in another expression.

sections.heading: Define the interface
sections.text: Read fn total(price: i64, quantity: i64) -> i64 as a function named total taking two signed integers and returning one signed integer. A parameter names a value inside the function. An argument is the value supplied by a call.

sections.heading: Trace a call
sections.text: In total(7, 3), price receives 7 and quantity receives 3. The function multiplies them, finishes, and the caller receives 21. The binding first keeps that result in main. The second call uses new arguments and its result is added to first.

sections.heading: Return from a block
sections.text: A final expression without a semicolon supplies the result. You can also write return price * quantity; to exit explicitly. A semicolon discards a final expression’s value. Keep an explicit return type on functions that return values when compiling a native executable.

sections.heading: Keep calculation separate from output
sections.text: total can serve a receipt, a test or a larger calculation because it returns its answer. main decides what to print. Parameters belong to each call. Declare a local mutable accumulator when you need a value to change inside the function.

exercise.prompt: Make the second order four units at four credits. Print the combined total for both orders.
exercise.hint: Only the second call in main needs different arguments.
exercise.answer: The first order is 21 and the second is 16. Their sum is 37.

title: While loops and the Euclidean algorithm
summary: Trace changing state and explain why a loop finishes.

sections.heading: Name the repeated work
sections.text: The greatest common divisor is the largest positive integer that divides both inputs exactly. For nonnegative inputs with at least one positive, dividing x by y leaves a remainder. A number divides both x and y exactly if and only if it divides y and that remainder.

sections.heading: Trace the state
sections.text: A while loop checks its condition before executing the body. Each pass replaces (x, y) with (y, x % y). Save the remainder first because overwriting x earlier would lose one of the inputs.

sections.heading: Explain termination
sections.text: When y is positive, the new remainder is at least zero and strictly smaller than y. Eventually y reaches zero. The guard prevents taking a remainder with a zero divisor and the final x supplies the answer.

sections.heading: Start with a small test
sections.text: If the second argument already equals zero, no iteration runs. Swapping positive inputs can add a first iteration, but the same common divisors survive. Tracing two small examples by hand is a quick way to find a mistaken update order.

exercise.prompt: Use 35 and 15 as inputs. Predict each remainder and the final result.
exercise.hint: Start with 35 % 15, then divide 15 by that remainder.
exercise.answer: The remainders are 5 and 0, so the last positive divisor is 5.

title: Break, continue and loop values
summary: Find the first matching integer and carry it out of a loop.

sections.heading: Choose a stopping rule
sections.text: while is convenient when the decision to repeat belongs at the top. Here the program must construct a candidate before it can decide whether to stop. A loop expression lets the test live beside the value that will become the answer.

sections.heading: Follow one iteration
sections.text: The counter starts at 9. The first pass increments it to 10. Its remainder on division by four is nonzero, so continue jumps back to the beginning. The update occurs before continue so the candidate moves forward on every pass.

sections.heading: Return a value from a loop
sections.text: At 12 the condition for continue is false. break n exits the nearest loop and supplies 12 to the binding found. The semicolon after the loop expression completes the enclosing let declaration. An ordinary break also exits a while loop, without carrying a value.

sections.heading: Distinguish the destinations
sections.text: continue returns to the next iteration, break leaves the current loop, and return leaves the current function. If your program stops with a step-budget error, trace the path through continue and check that the variable in the condition actually changes.

exercise.prompt: Find the first multiple of five strictly greater than nine.
exercise.hint: Keep the starting number and change the divisor.
exercise.answer: The first candidate is 10. Its remainder on division by five is zero, so it becomes the loop result.

title: Recursion and the cost of a call
summary: Trace Fibonacci by hand, identify the base case, and decide when iteration is cheaper.

sections.heading: Specify a base case
sections.text: In this example Fibonacci is defined on nonnegative integers with F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1. Each call first checks whether its argument is smaller than two. A base case gives a direct answer and prevents another call.

sections.heading: Expand one call
sections.text: For n = 4 the two subproblems are F(3) and F(2). F(3) needs F(2) and F(1), while each F(2) needs F(1) and F(0). Work back up the tree to get 2 + 1 = 3. Each invocation has its own parameter value.

sections.heading: Count work as well as depth
sections.text: F(2) is evaluated twice in that small tree. Repeated subproblems make this recursive implementation expensive as n grows. An iterative version can carry the two most recent values in mutable bindings and advance one position per pass.

sections.heading: Choose a safe input
sections.text: The interpreter has both a step budget and a maximum of 64 simultaneous calls. Keep practice inputs small. A native build also uses finite machine resources. Large Fibonacci numbers eventually exceed the checked i64 range regardless of the algorithm.

exercise.prompt: Print Fibonacci at position seven, with a matching label.
exercise.hint: The function name also occurs in the label. Edit the label and the call.
exercise.answer: Building the sequence from zero gives 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. Position seven is 13.

title: Vectors and reductions
summary: Represent several readings in one value and combine them into a weighted mean.

sections.heading: Choose a representation
sections.text: A vector literal such as [5.0, 7.0, 9.0] holds numeric elements in order. Element storage is f64, including when the literal contains whole numbers. A vector can be empty. Bind it to a name or pass it to a function whose parameter type is vector.

sections.heading: Read by position
sections.text: Indices begin at zero. For these three readings, len(readings) is 3 and at(readings, 2) is 9. Use an integer index and keep it below the length. The release supports reading vector elements. Build an accumulator when you need to calculate a derived result.

sections.heading: Give one reading extra weight
sections.text: A dot product multiplies pairs at matching positions and adds them. With weights [1.0, 1.0, 2.0], the weighted total is 5 + 7 + 18 = 30. The total weight is 4. Dividing produces 7.5, which is closer to the final reading than the ordinary mean.

sections.heading: State the input contract
sections.text: dot requires equal vector lengths. For a weighted average with nonnegative weights, require a positive total weight. An empty pair can have a valid dot product of zero while its mean has a zero denominator. Decide how your program should handle that case before you divide.

exercise.prompt: Give the first reading double weight and give each of the others weight one.
exercise.hint: Keep the number of weights equal to the number of readings.
exercise.answer: The weighted total becomes 10 + 7 + 9 = 26. Divide by four to get 6.5.

title: Scan a vector for its maximum
summary: Design a loop that finds the largest value even when every reading is negative.

sections.heading: Define the input
sections.text: Finding a maximum requires at least one reading. This example supplies a nonempty literal. A reusable function should check len(readings) before indexing, or document and enforce the nonempty requirement at its call site.

sections.heading: Choose a starting value
sections.text: Initialize peak from the first reading and begin the loop at index 1. Starting at zero as a candidate maximum would report a nonexistent zero for an all-negative input. The first real reading is a candidate you know belongs to the data.

sections.heading: Maintain a fact after every pass
sections.text: Before reading index i, peak is the largest of the first i elements. Compare the next reading with peak, keep the larger value and increment i. The same fact now covers one more element. When i equals len(readings), the fact covers the whole input.

sections.heading: Estimate the cost
sections.text: For n nonempty readings this scan performs n − 1 comparisons and stores a fixed number of local values beyond the input. A one-element vector skips the loop and returns its only element. Equal maxima do not change the reported value.

exercise.prompt: Try a vector containing just -12.0. Decide whether the loop body will run.
exercise.hint: After initialization the index and the vector length both equal one.
exercise.answer: The condition is false before the first pass. The initial reading is already the maximum.

title: Smooth a sequence with one running value
summary: Turn a noisy signal into a sequence of estimates and trace how much history each estimate retains.

sections.heading: Set the initial state
sections.text: The first reading is the first estimate. Print it before the loop and begin processing at index one. This convention gives one output per input, including for a single reading. The example assumes a nonempty signal because it reads index zero.

sections.heading: Blend old and new
sections.text: Each later estimate is half the new reading plus half the previous estimate. For readings 10, 14, 18, the second estimate is 0.5 × 14 + 0.5 × 10 = 12. The third uses 12 as its old state and becomes 15.

sections.heading: Understand the tradeoff
sections.text: More weight on the new reading makes the output respond faster to changes. Less weight preserves more history. Choose complementary weights that sum to one so a constant signal stays constant. A weight of one on the new reading reproduces the input.

sections.heading: Check a boundary case
sections.text: Feed the algorithm three copies of 6. Its estimate should remain 6 after every pass. This checks both the initial value and the blend. Then change one input at a time so the reason for any output change is visible.

exercise.prompt: Give the new reading weight 0.75 and the previous estimate weight 0.25.
exercise.hint: Both coefficients occur on the line that updates estimate.
exercise.answer: The second estimate is 13. The last uses 13 as its old state, yielding 16.75.

title: Fit a line and predict a value
summary: Fit a one-parameter model, inspect its assumptions, and predict the response at an unseen input.

sections.heading: Choose a model
sections.text: Suppose measurements are proportional to their input and a zero input should produce a zero response. Use y = slope × x. This choice fixes the intercept at zero. Pair each input with its observed target by position in two equal-length vectors.

sections.heading: Find the slope
sections.text: The least-squares slope through the origin is dot(samples, targets) / dot(samples, samples). The numerator adds input × observed response across the pairs. The denominator adds the squared inputs. It is positive when at least one input is nonzero.

sections.heading: Work a fit by hand
sections.text: With x = [1, 2, 3, 4] and y = [2, 4, 6, 8], the numerator is 60 and the denominator is 30. The slope is 2. A new input of 5 yields 10. The fit function only returns a coefficient. main chooses where to predict.

sections.heading: Interpret a changed observation
sections.text: Increase the last target by 3. The numerator increases by 4 × 3 while the denominator stays 30. The new slope is 72 / 30 = 2.4. One observation can move every future prediction because the fitted slope is shared.

exercise.prompt: Leave the training data unchanged and predict the response for x = 6.
exercise.hint: Change the final multiplication in main. The fit still sees the original four pairs.
exercise.answer: The fitted coefficient is still 2, and multiplying by 6 produces 12.

title: Measure prediction error
summary: Evaluate a set of predictions, trace the residuals and interpret their mean squared error.

sections.heading: Compare paired observations
sections.text: Take one prediction and the matching observed target. Their difference is a residual. Its sign tells you whether the prediction is high or low. Averaging signed residuals alone could hide errors that cancel one another.

sections.heading: Accumulate the loss
sections.text: With predictions [2, 3, 5] and targets [1, 4, 3], the residuals are 1, -1 and 2. Squaring gives 1, 1 and 4. Add the squares, then divide 6 by the number of observations, 3. The mean squared error is 2.

sections.heading: Match types and lengths
sections.text: The loop index is an integer for at. The floating-point count supplies a same-type divisor for squares in both execution paths. For inputs supplied by a caller, check that the lengths match and that at least one pair exists before you compute the mean.

sections.heading: Use held-out data
sections.text: Training chooses a slope or other parameters. Evaluation asks how those fixed parameters perform on examples that did not determine them. Keep a second vector of test targets when comparing two models. A low training loss alone says little about unseen observations.

exercise.prompt: Replace the predictions with the three actual targets. What is the best possible value of this loss?
exercise.hint: Each residual should be exactly zero for these inputs.
exercise.answer: All squared residuals are zero, so the mean squared error is zero.

title: Classify using a score and a threshold
summary: Combine two features, choose a category, and decide how ties are classified.

sections.heading: Build the score
sections.text: A feature is a numeric input such as a count or a measurement. A weight describes its contribution to a score. classify uses one weight per feature, computes dot(features, weights), then adds a scalar bias. The inputs and weights must have equal lengths.

sections.heading: Trace the prediction
sections.text: The two contributions are 2 × 0.5 = 1 and 3 × -0.25 = -0.75. With a zero bias the score is 0.25. The condition score >= 0.0 chooses the string positive. A negative sign on a weight makes a larger feature lower the score.

sections.heading: Choose the tie rule
sections.text: The comparison includes exactly zero on the positive side. A negative bias moves the cutoff without changing any individual weight. Test scores on both sides of zero and exactly at zero to check that the rule matches your intention.

sections.heading: Separate scoring from training
sections.text: This is inference with coefficients supplied in the program. There is no learning step in this classifier. If you choose different coefficients, evaluate their predictions on labeled data before interpreting the change as an improvement.

exercise.prompt: Set the bias to -0.5 and predict the label before running.
exercise.hint: The original weighted sum is 0.25.
exercise.answer: The adjusted score is -0.25. This selects the negative branch.

title: Test a program at its boundaries
summary: Design a small repeatable test suite that catches an off-by-one classification rule.

sections.heading: Write the rule first
sections.text: Raise an alarm only above 30.0. This sentence decides what happens at exactly 30.0. Implement the production rule in a function so the test calls precisely the same calculation that a larger program would use.

sections.heading: Choose three cases
sections.text: Select a value below the limit, exactly at the limit, and above it. For each input, compare the returned boolean with the expected boolean. A correct run prints true three times. If one line prints false, its position identifies the case to inspect.

sections.heading: Prove a test can fail
sections.text: Temporarily replace > with >= and run again. The below and above cases still pass. The equality case now prints false. Restore the strict comparison and repeat. This gives you evidence that at least one test can detect a real defect.

sections.heading: Compare execution paths
sections.text: Run the same source with blyxc run, then build an executable and compare its output on the same inputs. Checking the process exit status detects execution failures. Checking actual output against expected output detects wrong answers from executions that finished successfully.

exercise.prompt: Change the rule to include exactly 30 and update the expected result for that input.
exercise.hint: The implementation and the test expectation express two sides of the same contract.
exercise.answer: Both changes are needed to keep all three tests passing under the new specification.

title: Capstone project — build a sensor report
summary: Build a complete report from a blank file, handle empty input, and verify a boundary condition.

sections.heading: Specify the report
sections.text: Given a vector of readings and a limit, print their total and how many exceed the limit. For an empty batch, print no readings and stop. Before coding, write down the expected behavior for an empty batch, one reading equal to the limit, and a batch with readings on both sides.

sections.heading: Build the counting function
sections.text: Start with fn hot_count(readings: vector, limit: f64) -> i64. Start hits and i at zero. While i is less than len(readings), inspect at(readings, i). Increment hits only for a reading strictly above the limit. Advance i on every pass and return hits after the loop.

sections.heading: Build the report function
sections.text: Take the same two parameters. Check for an empty batch first. The early return lets the normal report follow at the same indentation. Use sum for the total, call hot_count for the count, and pair print! labels with println! values.

sections.heading: Trace and verify
sections.text: The four readings total 123.5. Only 31.5 and 34.0 exceed the limit of 30.0. The empty batch exercises a separate branch without reading an element. Verify the complete program in both the browser and the CLI.

sections.heading: Take it further
sections.text: Change the function to count readings inside an inclusive range. Accept low and high parameters and combine two comparisons with &&. Test both endpoints, a value outside each end, and an empty vector. Decide how a caller should handle low greater than high.

exercise.prompt: Replace only the empty batch in main with a single reading equal to the limit. Predict the complete report.
exercise.hint: This batch takes the nonempty branch but adds nothing to the above-limit count.
exercise.answer: The first batch is unchanged. For the second, sum returns 30 and the strict comparison leaves hits at zero.
exercise.expected:
total: 123.5
above limit: 2
total: 30
above limit: 0

title: Evaluate models with Blyx packages
summary: Compare the cost of two classifiers, check their probability forecasts, and score a ranked retrieval result. Run the comparison in CI or import the same Blyx functions into your application.

sections.heading: Start with a release decision
sections.text: You have predictions from two versions of a classifier on the same held-out observations. The current model raises one false alarm. Its replacement misses one positive. Both get three out of four right. Decide what a false alarm and a miss cost before you look at which model wins.

sections.heading: Prepare a paired CSV
sections.text: Save the four rows below as predictions.csv in UTF-8. Each row must refer to the same observation for both models. The label is 0 or 1. Each prediction is an unquoted number between 0 and 1. Keep the header and column order shown. Rows can use LF or CRLF line endings.

sections.heading: Run ModelGate
sections.text: ModelGate 0.1.2 ships as a native executable. On Apple Silicon macOS or x86-64 Linux use the Homebrew command below. On x64 Windows, extract the release ZIP from the ecosystem catalog and run .\modelgate.exe predictions.csv --fn-cost 5 in PowerShell. A release archive also contains fixtures/improved.csv and fixtures/regression.csv.

sections.heading: Read the decision
sections.text: At the default threshold of 0.5, a score equal to the threshold counts as positive. The baseline’s one false alarm costs 1. The candidate’s missed positive costs 5. Divide by four observations to get costs per row of 0.25 and 1.25. The JSON pass field is false. You can retain the report as a CI artifact using shell output redirection.

rows: Candidate meets the cost and Brier criteria.
The candidate exceeds at least one permitted limit.
The CSV, a value or a command option is invalid. Check the diagnostic.
The native host could not complete an I/O operation.

sections.heading: Measure probability quality
sections.text: Brier score averages the squared difference between each probability and its binary label. Two models with identical class decisions can have different Brier scores. ModelGate accepts --brier-tolerance for the largest allowed increase in this mean. The calibration library also provides cal_bin for counts, forecast totals and outcome totals, and cal_ece for a count-weighted summary of the gaps. Compare ECE on the same data using the same bin count.

sections.heading: Import a versioned library
sections.text: Install Blyx 0.2.1, Rust 1.85 or later and a platform linker for a source build. In an empty project directory, run the clone command below. It puts the release beside the entry file. For a shared project, record the commit in version control, for example as a Git submodule.

sections.heading: Use the library in a native program
sections.text: Save this code as main.blyx beside vendor and run blyxc native-run main.blyx. It prints 6, the total cost of one false alarm and one miss. To keep the executable use blyxc build main.blyx -o evaluate, or -o evaluate.exe on Windows. The editable browser program below contains the same library in one file.

sections.heading: Evaluate a retriever
sections.text: Use the retrieval package to score an ordered list of numeric document IDs for one judged query. With results [7, 7, 9], judgments [7, 9] and k of 3, unique hits occur at ranks 1 and 3. Precision is 2/3, recall is 1, reciprocal rank is 1, and average precision is (1 + 2/3) / 2. A repeated document still uses a rank. Record which queries have judgments and average the per-query metrics over that set.

sections.heading: Keep future data out of a time-series backtest
sections.text: Blyx Backtest measures forecasts in chronological folds. For demand [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80], set initial history to 3, forecast horizon to 2, gap to 1 and training window to 2. The first fold trains on 20 and 30, skips 40 and scores against 50 and 60. The next trains on 40 and 50, skips 60 and scores against 70 and 80. Across those four observations the last-value baseline has mean absolute error of 25, the training-mean baseline 30, and custom forecasts [45, 55, 65, 75] score 5. Use the same fold bounds when fitting preprocessing and model parameters.

sections.heading: Choose what to test
sections.text: Use held-out paired data and keep the error costs, threshold and tolerance fixed when comparing runs. Inspect the individual errors and the number of observations. The four-row fixture illustrates the decision rule. Statistical uncertainty, subgroup performance and business impact require evidence from your own evaluation.

exercise.prompt: In the worked program, raise the cost of a missed positive from 5 to 10. Predict the three lines of output and then run it.
exercise.hint: Only the total cost uses that argument. The confusion counts stay the same.
exercise.answer: Precision and recall both remain 0.5. One false alarm costs 1 and one missed positive now costs 10, so the final line is 11.

title: Train, calibrate and monitor a regression model
summary: Fit a regression, attach intervals using held-out errors, and catch persistent underprediction in a later stream. Run each stage in native Blyx or the browser.

sections.heading: Keep three sets of observations
sections.text: Use training pairs to fit the model. Reserve a separate calibration set for choosing an interval radius. Keep a stable, chronological reference period and later labelled predictions for monitoring. Reusing training errors for calibration can make intervals too narrow. Choose data splits before fitting.

sections.heading: Fit the relationship
sections.text: Save x,y pairs as a UTF-8 CSV. The second column is the response. The four rows below follow y = 2x + 1. The centered least-squares fit has feature mean 2.5, response mean 6 and slope 2. At x = 5 it predicts 11.

sections.heading: Run LinearFit
sections.text: Extract the LinearFit archive for your platform and run the included fixture. On Windows, start the command with .\linearfit.exe in PowerShell. On Apple Silicon macOS and x86-64 Linux you can also install it from the Blyx Homebrew tap. Supplying --ridge 5 shrinks the slope to 1 and changes the prediction to 8.5.

sections.heading: Train by batch or by row
sections.text: Use lf_fit on aligned vectors for a batch. For incoming observations start with lf_start, pass the state and next training pair to lf_update, and call lf_finish when you need a model. lf_merge combines disjoint training batches. The shared Moments library also exposes their means, centered sums and sample standard deviation.

sections.heading: Calibrate an interval
sections.text: Suppose a separate model predicted 10 for each of four calibration cases whose true values were 10, 12, 7 and 11. The absolute errors are 0, 2, 3 and 1. At target coverage 3/5, take the third smallest error because ceil((4+1)×3/5) = 3. This yields a radius of 2 and the interval [18,22] around a new prediction of 20. At 90% coverage four cases give no finite result.
sections.command:
let cal = cf_calibrate([10, 12, 7, 11], [10, 10, 10, 10], 3, 5);
let interval = cf_interval(20.0, at(cal, 0));

sections.heading: Interpret coverage
sections.text: Use cf_coverage on separate labelled predictions to measure the fraction inside the intervals. The usual split-conformal guarantee is marginal and assumes calibration and future examples are exchangeable. Inspect time periods or important subgroups separately when that assumption may fail.

sections.heading: Detect sustained underprediction
sections.text: ResidualWatch calculates actual minus predicted. In its shift fixture the first three residuals are −1, 0 and 1, so the frozen center is 0 and the sample scale is 1. Two later residuals of 2 add 1.5 each to the positive CUSUM at allowance 0.5. The second reaches the inclusive limit of 3. The first alert is data row 5, and the CLI exits with status 1.

sections.heading: Use alerts in a job
sections.text: Keep the JSON report from each run. Exit code 0 means the monitor finished without an alert, 1 means a limit was reached, 2 signals invalid input and 4 signals an I/O failure. Choose an allowance, limit and scale floor using a representative stable period. Investigate drift alarms against labels and feature changes before deciding whether to retrain.

sections.heading: Add a package to a native project
sections.text: With Blyx 0.2.1, Rust and a host linker installed, clone the tagged release next to your entry file. The training and monitoring packages include their pinned Blyx dependencies. Save the imported program as main.blyx and run blyxc native-run main.blyx. The package catalog has the exact import, function reference, runnable example and source for every package.

sections.heading: Run all three stages in one project
sections.text: The starter includes LinearFit, Conformal, ResidualWatch and their Blyx dependencies. With the native toolchain installed, extract the ZIP and run the command below in the project folder. The model predicts 21 with an interval from 19 to 23. The first incoming error gives a signal of 0. A second underprediction raises the signal to 1.

exercise.prompt: In the worked program, change the training penalty from 0 to 5. What happens to the slope and the prediction at x = 5?
exercise.hint: Sxx is 5 and Sxy is 10. The ridge slope divides Sxy by Sxx plus the penalty.
exercise.answer: The slope becomes 1. The centered prediction is 6 + 1 × (5 − 2.5), or 8.5.

title: Train a neural network with BlyxTorch
summary: Train an XOR classifier, inspect a real gradient, then compile a dense network for your own labels and deploy it as a standalone CPU executable.

sections.heading: Learn a nonlinear decision
sections.text: XOR labels the input pair (0,1) or (1,0) as positive. A single straight-line decision boundary cannot separate both positive points from the two negative points. The default BlyxTorch model uses two inputs, four tanh hidden units and one output logit. Its 17 parameters include all weights and biases.

sections.heading: Start in VS Code or VSCodium
sections.text: Install the BlyxTorch extension from your editor’s registry. It installs Blyx Language alongside the trainer. Create a file named sensor.blyx, type bt-sensor, accept the completion, and choose Blyx: Run File. Change the final sensor reading and run it again. An offline install uses the two VSIX files linked from the package page.

sections.heading: Train the released classifier
sections.text: Download and extract the matching archive. From its folder, run the three commands below. Training takes 250 epochs with Adam, a learning rate of 0.03, batches of four and seed 7. The output is a two-line text checkpoint. The prebuilt trainer runs directly. On Windows PowerShell, start commands with .\blyxtorch.exe and save the checkpoint with | Out-File -Encoding ascii xor.bt.
sections.command:
./blyxtorch train fixtures/xor.csv 250 0.03 4 adam 7 > xor.bt
./blyxtorch predict xor.bt fixtures/xor-features.csv
./blyxtorch score xor.bt fixtures/xor.csv

sections.heading: Read the predictions
sections.text: The mean training loss is about 0.00630 on the four rows. The probabilities below are rounded. To evaluate performance on a real dataset, keep separate labelled observations out of training and run score on those rows. In the browser example, change the second input from [0, 1] to [0, 0]. Its predicted class changes from true to false.

links.text: Run the trained XOR network in your browser

sections.heading: Trace a derivative
sections.text: The browser program uses a dual number with a value and a tangent. For a trainable weight use tangent 1; for a constant use tangent 0. At w = 1, the loss (2w − 5)² is 9. Its derivative is −12, so a gradient step with learning rate 0.125 moves the weight to 2.5 and the loss becomes zero.

sections.heading: Compile a different network
sections.text: Widths include input and output. This example uses eight and four hidden units for a three-class classifier. Compile the emitted Blyx source with Blyx 0.2.1, Rust 1.85 or later and a host linker. The resulting executable can train and predict on a different machine of the same target platform. For Windows PowerShell, send the emitted source through Out-File -Encoding ascii classifier.blyx and compile to classifier.exe.
sections.command:
./blyxtorch emit 2,8,4,3 softmax relu > classifier.blyx
blyxc build classifier.blyx -o classifier
./classifier --help

sections.heading: Choose a loss and a header
sections.text: Use mse for continuous targets, binary for one probability, or softmax for a single class index per observation. The input is an unquoted numerical UTF-8 CSV. Training and gradient commands use labelled rows. Prediction takes the feature columns alone.

sections.heading: Inspect gradients and checkpoints
sections.text: The gradient command returns a per-row loss followed by one derivative per trainable weight or bias. The compiled backward pass uses the chain rule to traverse the layers in reverse order. Within each layer the output-by-input weight matrix comes first in row-major order, then its bias vector. Loading checks the model's identity and parameter count. The optimizer uses the actual size of the final mini-batch.

sections.heading: Train and test on different jobs
sections.text: Extract the starter and open BlyxTorch.code-workspace. Each row describes pages divided by 100 and waiting jobs divided by 10. Select Terminal → Run Task → BlyxTorch: Evaluate print queue. The model trains on 16 synthetic jobs and evaluates six separate labels. The task reports six rows and mean loss near 0.00234. Edit new-jobs.csv and choose Predict new print jobs to score your inputs. A saved checkpoint and the browser program also run inference without retraining.
sections.command:
blyxtorch train-score print-queue/train.csv print-queue/holdout.csv 180 0.03 4 adam 7
blyxtorch train-predict print-queue/train.csv print-queue/new-jobs.csv 180 0.03 4 adam 7

sections.heading: Choose an appropriate workload
sections.text: BlyxTorch 0.2.0 runs fixed-shape float64 networks on CPU. It supports up to eight affine layers and 1,024 parameters. The published comparison covers five small networks, CPU PyTorch, and a separate CSV-scoring benchmark. GPU execution, convolution, transformer training and arbitrary-rank tensors are outside this release.

links.text: Compare the timings and measurement boundaries

exercise.prompt: In the worked program, change the learning rate from 0.125 to 0.25. Where does the update put the weight, and what loss do you get?
exercise.hint: The derivative before the update is −12. Compute 1 − 0.25 × (−12), then square the new prediction error.
exercise.answer: The weight becomes 4. Its prediction is 8, so the new loss is (8 − 5)² = 9. The larger step crosses the minimum.

title: Install and verify Blyx
summary: Choose a binary or package manager, locate the executable, and verify the exact compiler version.

sections.heading: Choose how to run the course
sections.text: Every tutorial with an editor can run in the browser. A local installation lets you save source files and invoke the command-line tool blyxc. Building a native executable also requires rustc and a host linker on the machine doing the build.

sections.heading: Download a release archive
sections.text: Choose the Windows x86-64 ZIP, Linux x86-64 tarball, or Apple Silicon macOS tarball from the download page. Compare its SHA-256 digest with the entry for the same filename in SHA256SUMS. Extract the archive and add the directory containing blyxc to PATH. In PowerShell you can run .\blyxc.exe directly from the extracted directory.

sections.heading: Install with Homebrew
sections.text: On Apple Silicon macOS or x86-64 Linux, the project tap installs the published compiler binary and checks the archive checksum.

sections.heading: Install on Windows with Scoop
sections.text: On Windows x64, add the project bucket once from PowerShell, then install the compiler and check its version. Scoop checks the release archive against the SHA-256 in the manifest. You can also install the native AI commands with scoop install blyx/linearfit blyx/residualwatch blyx/modelgate.
sections.command:
scoop bucket add blyx https://github.com/Rahulchaube1/scoop-blyx
scoop install blyx/blyx
blyxc --version

sections.heading: Install with Cargo
sections.text: With Rust, Cargo and a host linker installed, build the compiler from crates.io. The version flag selects the same release as this course. Cargo normally places the result in the bin directory under your Cargo home.

sections.heading: Check your installation
sections.text: Open a fresh terminal after a PATH change. The version command should print blyxc 0.2.1. If the shell cannot find it, check the directory from which the executable runs directly and make sure that directory appears on PATH.

exercise.prompt: Confirm which compiler your terminal will use if you have both a downloaded binary and a Cargo installation.
exercise.hint: Use Get-Command blyxc in PowerShell or command -v blyxc in a POSIX shell.
exercise.answer: The path should point to the installation you intended. Run that path with --version to verify it before continuing.

title: Create a project on disk
summary: Move a program from the browser into a project, check the file and run it from a terminal.

sections.heading: Create a workspace
sections.text: Choose a parent directory where you want to keep your work. This command creates a fresh directory named hello. Blyx refuses to create the project if that directory already exists, which helps protect existing work.

sections.heading: Find the entry point
sections.text: The generated project contains Blyx.toml and src/main.blyx. The manifest records the project name, version and edition. The released CLI takes an explicit source file. Open hello/src/main.blyx in a text editor and find fn main().

sections.heading: Check, run and edit
sections.text: From the same parent directory, run these commands in order. check parses the source. run executes it. The starter prints Hello, Blyx! Replace its print call with a calculation, save the file and run it again.
sections.command:
blyxc check hello/src/main.blyx
blyxc run hello/src/main.blyx

sections.heading: Keep paths consistent
sections.text: If you change directory into hello, write src/main.blyx in subsequent commands. A file-not-found message is often a working-directory issue. The formatter rewrites the named file with normalized line endings.

sections.heading: Add a package to a native project
sections.text: Clone a tagged Blyx library beside your entry file and import its public functions with use. The native runner and native build follow these local paths. The “Evaluate models with Blyx packages” chapter builds a working example. A Git submodule or a recorded commit keeps the dependency reproducible.

exercise.prompt: Make the starter print 21. Run a syntax check first and then execute the saved file.
exercise.hint: In main, multiply 3 by 7 inside println!.
exercise.answer: Use println!(3 * 7); and save. A successful check reports that the file parsed. The run command prints 21.

title: Develop in VS Code
summary: Run an unsaved editor buffer, read a parser diagnostic and move the same program to the CLI.

sections.heading: Open a Blyx file
sections.text: Install the desktop extension with ID RahulChaube.blyx-language. Open or create a file ending in .blyx. For an untitled buffer, select Blyx as its language. The editor highlighting helps you see strings, keywords and comments.

sections.heading: Run the active buffer
sections.text: Use the play button in the editor title bar or choose Blyx: Run File in the Command Palette. The Blyx output channel shows the output for the current text, including unsaved edits. Paste the first tutorial program and change the string to confirm which version is running.

sections.heading: Read a diagnostic
sections.text: Remove the closing brace of main and look in the Problems panel. A parser diagnostic reports where parsing ran into trouble. Restore the brace, wait for the parser to update and run again. Runtime failures, such as a zero integer divisor, appear when the program executes.

sections.heading: Use a local extension file
sections.text: For an offline installation, download blyx-language-1.2.3.vsix from the editor release and choose Install from VSIX in the Extensions view. The extension uses a bundled WebAssembly interpreter. Save the source to disk before running a CLI command against that file.

exercise.prompt: Change a string without saving. Compare an editor run with a terminal run before and after saving.
exercise.hint: The editor reads the buffer. The terminal reads the file on disk.
exercise.answer: Before saving, the editor can print the new string while the CLI prints the old one. Save and run both again to compare the same source.

title: Debug and recover from errors
summary: Locate a syntax error, diagnose a runtime failure, and guard an operation using short-circuit evaluation.

sections.heading: Identify the failing stage
sections.text: Check the file path first. A syntax error occurs while reading the program structure. A runtime error occurs while executing a valid expression with particular values. An error from a native build can point to a type mismatch or a missing Rust toolchain.

rows: Missing punctuation or an unfinished expression
Inspect that token and the preceding statement.
The index fell outside the vector
Check 0 <= i and i < len(v) before at.
dot requires vectors of equal length
The inputs contain different numbers of observations
Trace the loop condition and its updates.

sections.heading: Reproduce the smallest failure
sections.text: Save fn main() { println!(1 / 0); } as divide.blyx. A syntax check succeeds because the expression is well formed. Running it reports an integer division error and exits with code 4. Replace the zero with 2 and rerun. Whole-number division now prints 0.

sections.heading: Put a guard before division
sections.text: The example reads count != 0 && total / count > 3. With a zero count the first comparison is false, so evaluation skips the division. Reversing the operands would evaluate the division before discovering the zero.

sections.heading: Limit a test run
sections.text: A runaway loop can repeatedly evaluate valid code. Use a small positive budget while investigating it. The released interpreter also enforces a separate call-depth limit. Increasing the budget only helps after you have confirmed that the computation progresses.

exercise.prompt: Make the second call use a nonzero count whose integer quotient is exactly three.
exercise.hint: Keep total at 12 and choose a count that divides it evenly.
exercise.answer: The quotient 12 / 4 is 3. The strict > 3 comparison returns false, and the zero-count case also returns false.

title: Build a native executable
summary: Compile a typed Blyx program and compare the executable with the interpreter on the same input.

sections.heading: Start with a known result
sections.text: Run the project source through the interpreter and keep a small expected output. When trying a native build for the first time, use the generated hello project or the capstone. Both have simple results that you can check by eye.

sections.heading: Build for your host
sections.text: Install a Rust compiler and host linker. From inside your Blyx project, run the command below. The native backend translates supported Blyx syntax to Rust and invokes rustc to produce an optimized executable for the build machine.

sections.heading: Choose the output location
sections.text: An explicit output name makes scripts easier to read. On Linux or macOS, run the executable using a relative path. Use a separate output path from the source file.

sections.heading: Build on Windows
sections.text: In PowerShell, use an .exe suffix and the current-directory prefix. The resulting executable runs independently of blyxc and rustc on a compatible machine.

sections.heading: Compare the two paths
sections.text: Give numeric operands matching types and add explicit return types to functions that return values. The interpreter can promote mixed integer/float operations that a native build rejects. Check the executable's output using the same ordinary and boundary inputs you used for the interpreted run.

sections.heading: Build a program with imports
sections.text: Native builds resolve local use paths and built-in host modules. The native runner builds the program and runs it in one step. Put program arguments after --. Use a normal build to keep an executable for repeated runs.

exercise.prompt: Build the capstone source as a native executable, run it and compare the complete output with the chapter’s expected output.
exercise.hint: Save the complete capstone program to src/main.blyx first.
exercise.answer: The four readings sum to 123.5, two exceed 30, and the empty call prints no readings. Those three lines should agree across both execution paths.

title: Syntax, types and operators
summary: Look up the executable forms, operator order and value types used in Blyx 0.2.1.

sections.heading: Read the shape of a program
sections.text: A runnable source file declares top-level functions, including a parameterless main. A function body is a brace-delimited block of statements and an optional final expression. A semicolon ends a let declaration, return statement or expression statement. A final expression without one supplies the block’s value.

sections.heading: Read names, literals and comments
sections.text: Choose a name such as sensor_count. Start with a letter or underscore and use letters, digits or underscores after it. Names are case-sensitive. The lexer reads 10, 0b1010, 0o12 and 0xA as the same integer. Use underscores to group long numbers and e for a decimal exponent. A line comment begins with //. A block comment begins with /* and ends with */. Block comments may nest.

sections.heading: Value types
sections.text: Use explicit scalar types for native function parameters and results. Vector elements are numeric. A unit-valued block completes without returning a useful value.

rows: Checked integer arithmetic, counts and indices
Measurements, division with fractions and vector elements
Text, labels and messages. The native subset also recognizes String.
An immutable sequence of numeric elements
A function called for its effect

sections.heading: Operator order
sections.text: The rows are ordered from tightest binding to loosest among the operators used by the released interpreter here. Parentheses override the default order. Keep comparisons separate and join their boolean results with && or ||.

sections.heading: Declarations and control flow
sections.text: let binds, let mut permits updates and fn introduces a function. if selects a branch, while checks before each pass, and loop repeats unconditionally. break leaves the nearest loop, continue begins its next iteration, and return exits the current function. Nested braces introduce a scope.

sections.heading: Literal and boundary behavior
sections.text: The signed integer range is −9,223,372,036,854,775,808 through 9,223,372,036,854,775,807. Integer overflow and division by zero fail in the interpreter. f64 has finite precision and follows IEEE floating-point arithmetic. Many decimal fractions have only approximate binary representations. For native examples, use decimal literals consistently when a fractional result matters.

sections.heading: Text and escape sequences
sections.text: Write strings in double quotes. Inside a string, \n starts a new line, \t inserts a tab, \" inserts a quote, and \\ inserts a backslash. Strings may contain Unicode text. Use several print! calls to combine text with values. The interpreter also reads a single-quoted character as one character of text. Use double-quoted text in code you plan to build natively.

sections.heading: Use a branch as a value
sections.text: The classify function below uses if and else to produce a result. Both branch blocks end in string expressions and have the same result type. show returns unit and exists to print the result. The explicit -> unit annotation may be omitted there. Function parameters and any native return values use the types in the table above.

exercise.prompt: Change the classifier call to use the integer eleven in hexadecimal. Predict the final line and check whether the other lines change.
exercise.hint: In hexadecimal, the digits after 9 are A, B, C, D, E and F. Eleven divided by two leaves a remainder of one.
exercise.answer: 0xB is eleven. classify chooses the odd branch, and the earlier calculations still use the original literals.

title: Built-in functions and output
summary: Look up every vector built-in and both output macros, including their inputs, results and boundary cases.

sections.heading: Vector operations
sections.text: All four functions receive vectors by value in Blyx source. The interpreter shares immutable element storage across calls. An index is an i64; an element, sum or dot product is an f64.

rows: i64 count, zero for an empty vector
The element at a zero-based index
Sum of products at matching indices

sections.heading: Preconditions
sections.text: at fails on a negative index, on index len(v), and on any access to an empty vector. dot fails if lengths differ, even when one side is empty. The sum of an empty vector and the dot product of two empty vectors are numerically zero. Check lengths before indexing or computing an average.

sections.heading: Output macros
sections.text: print!() emits no text. println!() emits a newline. With a single expression, print!(value) displays its value, and println!(value) follows it with a newline. Use consecutive calls to combine text and numbers. Braces inside an output string are literal characters.

sections.heading: Cost of the operations
sections.text: Reading the length or one element requires no scan. sum and dot visit the elements and their work grows with vector length. The interpreter charges its execution budget for these reductions. Holding the sum in a binding avoids recomputing it in every loop iteration.

exercise.prompt: Calculate dot([2.0, -1.0], [3.0, 4.0]) by hand. What happens if you remove the 4.0 from the second vector?
exercise.hint: Multiply the corresponding entries before summing.
exercise.answer: 2 × 3 + (−1 × 4) is 2. After removing an entry the lengths differ, and the runtime reports an error.

title: Command-line reference
summary: Look up CLI forms, output files, execution budgets and exit codes.

sections.heading: Command forms
sections.text: Pass the entry file to each command. Native builds and native-run also load its local imports. Quote any path containing spaces as required by your shell.

rows: Create a new directory with Blyx.toml and src/main.blyx.
Parse the file and report syntax diagnostics.
Interpret main with an optional positive step budget.
Build a native executable, optionally at PATH.
Build the native project, run it and forward the program arguments.
Rewrite the file with normalized line endings.

sections.heading: Interpret the exit status
sections.text: Capture the exit status immediately following the command. In PowerShell read $LASTEXITCODE. In a POSIX shell read $?. Scripts can use the status to decide whether to proceed. The exit codes below describe blyxc itself.

rows: Examples include a missing file, parser error or failed build.
Examples include an unknown command, a missing argument or an invalid run budget.
The interpreter reached a runtime failure, such as integer division by zero.

sections.heading: Find the output file
sections.text: With no -o option a native build puts the executable beside the source, using the platform executable extension. Pass an explicit output name when a project has several programs or when a script needs to invoke a known path.

sections.heading: Separate execution budgets
sections.text: --max-steps controls a CLI interpreter run. The browser and the VS Code worker also enforce source, output and time limits. A native executable has ordinary process and system limits. These modes can differ for a very long or deeply recursive computation.

exercise.prompt: Choose the commands for a script that first checks the syntax of main.blyx, then runs it with a budget of 500 steps.
exercise.hint: Check the exit status before starting the second command.
exercise.answer: Use blyxc check main.blyx, followed on success by blyxc run main.blyx --max-steps 500. A parser success does not guarantee that execution will finish within the budget.

title: What Blyx 0.2.1 can run
summary: Choose an execution mode and identify features that are still being developed.

sections.heading: Choose an execution mode
sections.text: Use the CLI interpreter or browser for immediate feedback. Use a native build to distribute a supported typed program to a compatible host. The editor and playground run the interpreter compiled to WebAssembly.

rows: A complete source buffer with fn main()
256 KiB source, 64 KiB output and an eight-second worker deadline.
A .blyx file and the blyxc executable
Default one million evaluation steps and at most 64 simultaneous calls.
A supported typed program, rustc and a host linker
The generated program runs with system resources; interpreter step and call budgets do not apply.

sections.heading: Supported execution
sections.text: The teaching examples use functions, local bindings, scalar arithmetic, loops, recursion, numeric vectors and print macros. Native programs can import local .blyx modules and read command-line arguments or UTF-8 files through the host library. Use native-run or build for multi-file applications.

sections.heading: Features under development
sections.text: The package registry and its dependency resolver are prototypes. The published source libraries use versioned Git checkouts. The browser and CLI interpreter execute a single source buffer. GPU kernels, a general tensor runtime, asynchronous tasks and actor scheduling remain development work.

sections.heading: Interpret a benchmark
sections.text: Measure the same workload, input size and output across the implementations you compare. Separate startup costs from computational work when they answer different questions. The project’s published Fibonacci benchmark includes startup and reports its machine, raw samples and methodology.

exercise.prompt: Decide how to deliver a small numeric utility to a colleague who has no compiler installed. What do you need on each machine?
exercise.hint: Distinguish the machine doing the build from the machine running the result.
exercise.answer: On a suitable build host use blyxc, rustc and a linker to build the typed source. Deliver the executable for your colleague’s compatible OS and architecture. Try a small known input on the destination machine.
